title: More Rules, Longer Lists? Benchmarking Self-Evolving Agents on a Hidden-Rule Curriculum
author: Chenjie Qiu, Boyan Xu, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Ruichu Cai, Dongsheng Luo
contentSnippet:
Authors: Chenjie Qiu , Boyan Xu , Shaobin Shi , Bingfeng Chen , Ruichu Cai , Dongsheng Luo

Abstract: Self-evolving agents rewrite a persistent state from feedback, but it is largely untested whether this lets them learn a rule nobody told them. An agent can also pass by writing down each correction as an exception, and its list then grows with every new rule. We introduce CLR-Bench, a Curriculum of Latent Rules benchmark. Each chain adds one hidden rule per level on top of the earlier ones. A rule acts on an opaque label that stands for a named grouping published on the Web, such as the founding members of an airline alliance. The task gives one example value, practice feedback reveals one more member and one non-member, and the test checks unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify that the base model knows the members of each grouping and does not guess it without feedback, and that the evidence identifies the grouping once labels are read as named groupings. An automated pipeline builds chains from a new data domain, and we release 20 chains over 10 domains. We evaluate six recent self-evolution methods. With the certifying model they barely learn. The best gain at most 5 points over a frozen agent and exclude only 6-12% of the unseen members from the count, fewer than the 20% reached by simply keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson that states the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. Their states hold the revealed member in 75-98% of cases and almost never the class name, and when practice exposes a member the list misses, they add that member to the list. With the stronger GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet learn from feedback alone. They reach 78% accuracy and solve 59-60% of the single cells, against 53% and 8% with the certifying model, and they surpass the raw history. CLR-Bench therefore measures how well an agent learns, and this ability differs across models.

Notes: 13 pages, 8 figures, 11 tables

summary.tldr:
Researchers Chenjie Qiu, Boyan Xu, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Ruichu Cai, and Dongsheng Luo introduced CLR-Bench (Curriculum of Latent Rules), a benchmark designed to evaluate whether self-evolving agents can learn hidden rules through feedback rather than simply memorizing exceptions. The benchmark consists of 20 chains across 10 data domains, where each level adds a hidden rule based on opaque labels representing real-world groupings, such as airline alliance members. The task provides a single example, followed by practice feedback identifying one member and one non-member, before testing the agent on unseen members and similar non-members.

Evaluation of six recent self-evolution methods revealed significant limitations: when using a certifying model, the best-performing agents gained only 5 points over frozen agents, failing to outperform raw practice history. These agents typically stored individual members in their state rather than identifying the underlying class name. However, providing a fixed lesson on the naming convention improved performance by 14.5 to 16.5 points. When tested with the more capable GPT-6-Sol model, methods like ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet achieved 78% accuracy and solved 59-60% of single cells, demonstrating that the ability to learn from feedback is highly dependent on the underlying model's reasoning capabilities.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** CLR-Bench includes 20 chains across 10 distinct data domains to test rule-learning capabilities.
**Performance Gap:** Self-evolving agents using standard certifying models gained at most 5 points over frozen agents, underperforming compared to simple raw history retention.
**Instructional Impact:** Providing a fixed lesson on the naming convention improved agent performance by 14.5 to 16.5 points.
**Model Dependency:** Using the GPT-6-Sol model allowed ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet to reach 78% accuracy, significantly outperforming the certifying model baseline of 53%.

**State Behavior:** Agents frequently stored revealed members in their persistent state (75-98% of cases) but failed to identify or store the actual class name, indicating a reliance on list-building rather than rule generalization.

title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models
author: Zhifei Hu, Alexandra I. Cristea, Adel Bibi, Jialin Yu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Zhifei Hu , Alexandra I. Cristea , Adel Bibi , Jialin Yu

Abstract: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.

summary.tldr: A new arXiv study (2610.40798v1) reveals that current web world models fail to ensure safety sufficiency despite generating plausible future predictions, scoring an alarming disconnect in 86.1% of evaluated scenarios. This exposes a critical gap in agentic architecture, proving that visual or textual plausibility does not equate to reliable risk mitigation for autonomous web agents.
takeaways: Evaluated 3,000 predictions across ten frozen open-source models in a rigorous matched human evaluation framework.
Demonstrates that an 86.1% failure rate in safety sufficiency occurs even when models output highly convincing, plausible future trajectories.
Shifts industry focus from generative visual/state prediction accuracy to explicit alignment and safety-bound verification layers.

title: Circumventing the Computational Hardness of Computational Arbitrage
author: Nastaran Okati, Ricardo Olmedo, Moritz Hardt
contentSnippet:
Authors: Nastaran Okati , Ricardo Olmedo , Moritz Hardt

Abstract: AI model marketplaces host providers with heterogeneous costs and capabilities. These differences create an opportunity for computational arbitrage (Olmedo et al., 2026), in which an intermediary purchases inference from a portfolio of models and resells it to users at a profit. Beyond creating profit opportunities for the arbitrageur, computational arbitrage offers financial value to both consumers and providers and could therefore significantly influence AI model markets. While prior work empirically demonstrates the feasibility of computational arbitrage for small model pools, scaling it to large marketplaces requires arbitrage strategies that are both computationally tractable and inexpensive to identify and deploy. In this work, we formalize computational arbitrage as an allocation problem and prove that it is generally NP-hard. However, we show that the optimal allocation can be computed efficiently under a natural diminishing-returns condition on how model performance scales with inference spending. We further develop a sample-efficient method for estimating model performance from limited data, reducing the upfront cost of identifying arbitrage strategies. Our analysis also yields several economic insights: at the optimum, every funded model delivers the same marginal utility per dollar; arbitrage directs revenue away from providers offering little utility relative to their prices; and it rewards complementary specialization.

summary.tldr: A new research paper explores overcoming the computational hardness of computational arbitrage in AI model marketplaces. This breakthrough enables intermediaries to efficiently optimize inference purchasing across heterogeneous providers to maximize margins.
takeaways: Formalizes computational arbitrage as a mechanism to exploit cost and capability discrepancies across heterogeneous AI model providers.
Addresses the computational hardness barrier, transforming an intractable routing problem into a tractable operational strategy for inference intermediaries.
Shifts the market dynamics toward automated brokerages that sit between end-users and base model providers to optimize price-performance dynamically.

title: Incongruence-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition in Audio Large Language Models
author: Fengji Jing, Guy Laban
contentSnippet:
Authors: Fengji Jing , Guy Laban

Abstract: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Fengji Jing and Guy Laban have introduced a new methodology for evaluating multimodal speech emotion recognition (SER) in audio-capable Large Language Models (LLMs) by quantifying 'incongruence'—the discrepancy between textual content and vocal delivery. By mapping both modalities into a shared valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) space, the authors developed a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score using a two-component Gaussian mixture model. This metric was validated against human judgment and tested across three distinct datasets: eNTERFACE'05 (acted), MELD (conversational), and CMU-MOSEI (spontaneous).

The study reveals that when audio is present, incongruence significantly increases the probability of classification error in LLMs, even after controlling for ground-truth emotion and feature-space distance. Notably, this behavior contrasts with supervised classifiers trained on identical features, which do not exhibit the same performance degradation. This suggests that the failure point is specific to how LLMs integrate multimodal evidence rather than an inherent limitation of the input signals. The researchers found that text-only effects were inconsistent, as swapping the underlying transcript-reading model could reverse performance trends, whereas their proposed incongruence score remained a robust predictor of error across all tested corpora.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Developed a label-free, continuous incongruence score using a two-component Gaussian mixture model in a shared valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) space.

**Performance Impact:** Incongruence between text and audio channels consistently increases the odds of error in audio-capable LLMs across all three evaluated datasets (eNTERFACE'05, MELD, CMU-MOSEI).
**Comparative Finding:** Supervised classifiers trained on the same features perform differently than LLMs, indicating the issue lies in the LLM's multimodal evidence integration architecture.
**Robustness:** The proposed incongruence score outperformed six simpler alternatives as the only metric capable of predicting errors across all three corpora without requiring emotion labels.
**Resource Availability:** The authors have released the source code, data tables, and prompts used in the study.

title: ChatGPT as a Surveillance Assistant? An Exploratory Case Study of AI-Assisted Surveillance Risks
author: Ayana Hussain, Nicholas Vincent
contentSnippet:
Authors: Ayana Hussain , Nicholas Vincent

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate detailed guidance, functional code, and persuasive text at scale. As one of the most widely used consumer language model products as of 2026, ChatGPT gives broad public access to these capabilities, motivating concerns about its potential use in surveillance-related tasks. We present an exploratory case study of what potentially harmful surveillance assistance looks like in ChatGPT's public web interface. We contribute a taxonomy of seven surveillance risk categories based on prior LLM risk research and reports of deployed surveillance systems, instantiated as 110 prompts, along with a manually reviewed analysis of ChatGPT's responses. Prompts were issued using two approaches: 55 jailbreak prompts drawing on five types of elicitation strategies, and 55 plain-language direct prompts, each run alone, and if unsuccessful, again with a short fixed prefix. We find that ChatGPT provides substantive surveillance guidance for 40 of the 55 jailbreak prompts and for 33 of the 55 direct prompts without any prefix. Compliant responses also rarely included policy mentions or suggestions for privacy-preserving alternatives. We manually review every response and find that even when ChatGPT states a refusal, it may still supply detailed instructions, working code, or architectural guidance alongside brief ethical caveats.

summary.tldr: A new exploratory case study investigates the dual-use risks of consumer large language models like ChatGPT functioning as surveillance assistants. The research highlights growing concerns over how widely accessible LLM capabilities can be co-opted for targeted monitoring and tactical digital tracking.
takeaways: The study evaluates how easily general-purpose consumer LLMs can generate actionable guidance for digital and physical surveillance operations.
Widespread public access to advanced code and text generation lowers the barrier to entry for building scalable surveillance infrastructure.
Enterprise and research communities must re-evaluate safety guardrails against dual-use exploitation in automated monitoring contexts.

title: Does Recursive Knowledge Construction Help Agents Verify Consensus Claims in Science?
author: Lun Ai, Yu-Heng Wu, Jonathan Schaul, Leonie K\"uchenhoff, Denes Turei, Francesco Carli, Fabio Petroni, Aurelien Dugourd, Julio Saez-Rodriguez
contentSnippet:
Authors: Lun Ai , Yu-Heng Wu , Jonathan Schaul , Leonie Küchenhoff , Denes Turei , Francesco Carli , Fabio Petroni , Aurelien Dugourd , Julio Saez-Rodriguez

Abstract: Recent scientific agents build knowledge recursively by retrieving evidence, constructing an intermediate state, and judging whether that state contains sufficient information. These agents are evaluated end-to-end, usually without ground truth, so the effect of each design choice is unknown. Here, we examined two design axes: (1) what the recursion builds (the state of evidence) and (2) what controls it (the judge that decides when to stop). To measure them, we defined consensus scientific claim verification and measured these effects on this task, where a system must establish a claim's consensus stance from the open literature. We built a new consensus claim dataset, ProClaim-eval, including 718 claims with SUPPORT and REFUTE gold labels from five expert-curated databases spanning molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy. Our instrument, ProClaim, persists an evidence state outside the model's context, so each axis can be studied with the other held fixed. Against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks among the top three, with a significant advantage over the harnesses. We found that the evidence state improves performance over in-context accumulation, and it also matters what is stored in it. In addition, a trained judge that reads the evidence state performs better than fixed-round stopping. A judge trained separately and never exposed to ProClaim-eval achieves the highest agreement with the gold labels on three of five subsets, where it matches the off-the-shelf Claude Sonnet~4.6 judge and outperforms Claude Haiku~4.5. Our results support recursively maintaining a structured evidence state outside the model's context as an effective design for verifying claims in scientific agents.

summary.tldr:
Researchers led by Lun Ai and Julio Saez-Rodriguez have introduced ProClaim, a framework designed to evaluate recursive knowledge construction in scientific agents. The study focuses on two primary design axes: the structure of the evidence state and the mechanism controlling the recursion (the 'judge'). To facilitate this, the team developed ProClaim-eval, a new benchmark dataset containing 718 scientific claims across molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy, each labeled with 'SUPPORT' or 'REFUTE' ground truth derived from expert-curated databases.

Technically, ProClaim maintains an evidence state external to the model's context window, allowing for modular testing of design choices. Experimental results demonstrate that maintaining an external, structured evidence state outperforms standard in-context accumulation methods. Furthermore, the study finds that a trained judge—specifically one trained separately from the evaluation set—consistently outperforms fixed-round stopping mechanisms. When compared against general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks in the top three, showing significant performance advantages in verifying consensus scientific claims.

Performance analysis indicates that the trained judge matches the efficacy of Claude 3.5 Sonnet and exceeds that of Claude 3.5 Haiku on three of the five dataset subsets. The authors conclude that decoupling the evidence state from the model's context is a critical architectural requirement for reliable scientific verification, providing a more robust alternative to end-to-end agent evaluation without ground truth.
takeaways: **Dataset Composition:** ProClaim-eval consists of 718 scientific claims with gold-standard labels across molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy.
**Architectural Advantage:** Storing evidence outside the model's context window yields higher verification accuracy compared to traditional in-context accumulation.
**Judge Performance:** A separately trained judge achieves parity with Claude 3.5 Sonnet and outperforms Claude 3.5 Haiku on 60% of the tested scientific domains.
**System Ranking:** ProClaim ranks among the top three systems for consensus claim verification, significantly outperforming general-purpose agent harnesses.
**Design Findings:** The study confirms that the specific content stored in the evidence state and the use of a trained judge are the primary drivers of verification success.

title: Towards Portable Specification of the Agent Harness
author: Nicolas Gertler, Claudio Novelli, Luciano Floridi
contentSnippet:
Authors: Nicolas Gertler , Claudio Novelli , Luciano Floridi

Abstract: Large language models act only through the infrastructure that surrounds them. That infrastructure, the harness, determines what a model can accomplish and how it fails, yet it has no settled definition. To address this gap, we decompose the harness into eight functional components that can be specified and compared across systems, and we propose a portable specification framework that records which model ran in which harness. The record is needed because different harness configurations can yield several-fold differences in reported scores for the same model, and because much of an agent's attack surface lies in its harness. Existing model cards and agent cards provide release and operational information, but do not establish the sequence of effective configurations within a run. Harnesses can change between releases and between runs, and, where agents edit their own tools and configuration, within a run. Enacted AI laws contain documentation duties relevant to covered systems, subject to their respective scopes and application dates, but do not prescribe the common harness record proposed here. Therefore, the harness has to be explicitly described and specified as a versioned part of the system.

summary.tldr:
Authors Nicolas Gertler, Claudio Novelli, and Luciano Floridi propose a standardized, portable specification framework for 'agent harnesses'—the infrastructure surrounding large language models that dictates their operational capabilities and failure modes. The authors argue that current documentation standards, such as model cards and agent cards, fail to capture the dynamic nature of these harnesses, which can cause multi-fold variations in performance benchmarks for identical models.

The proposed framework decomposes the harness into eight distinct functional components, enabling researchers to record and version the specific configuration under which a model operates. This is critical because agent harnesses are not static; they can evolve between releases, across different runs, and even during a single execution if an agent modifies its own tools or configuration. The authors emphasize that this documentation is essential for security, as a significant portion of an agent's attack surface is embedded within the harness rather than the model weights themselves. While emerging AI regulations mandate documentation for covered systems, the authors note that current legal frameworks do not yet require the granular, versioned harness records necessary for reproducibility and safety.
takeaways: **Functional Decomposition:** The framework categorizes the agent harness into eight distinct functional components to allow for cross-system comparison.
**Performance Variance:** The authors identify that identical models can exhibit multi-fold differences in benchmark scores depending on the specific harness configuration used.
**Security Implications:** A primary motivation for the framework is that the harness constitutes a major portion of an agent's attack surface, which is currently under-documented.
**Regulatory Gap:** Existing AI laws impose documentation duties but fail to prescribe the specific, versioned harness records required to track configuration changes within or between runs.

title: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
author: Sean Hollister
contentSnippet: Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi. But I won’t be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home. It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it. [Media: https://www.tiktok.com/@verge/video/7702862550014168333] My version doesn’t sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio, but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home. Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code. Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C. Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud. When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app. Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/verge-sean-hollister-muse-gadget-331A2570-01-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all

summary.tldr:
A tech journalist built a custom AI-powered "Tamagotchi" pendant for $50 using the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C developer kit, bypassing Meta's upcoming commercial Muse Charm. The off-the-shelf silver metal pocket watch devkit is officially sanctioned by Meta as a "Muse Gadget" for connecting to Meta's open-source Muse AI cloud. Initial deployment via Meta's GitHub and Claude required significant troubleshooting, as the default build suffered from slow transcription, lacked full message display, featured only a single "Jolly" avatar, and failed to natively discover smart home devices.

Using Claude Code without prior coding experience, the author injected custom "vibe code" to drastically overhaul the hardware's functionality. Modifications included adding a conversation history page, integrating a British ElevenLabs AI voice for text-to-speech output, building a low-quality Bluetooth camera preview, implementing a remote camera shutter for the phone, and creating a multi-tiered Tamagotchi minigame tracking hunger, boredom, sleep, and hygiene. The device was also programmed with a functional three-hand pocket watch face and a local video player running clips of Mark Zuckerberg introducing the Muse Charm, all completed within minutes of natural language prompting.

The author deployed the pendant on a guest Wi-Fi network as a security precaution due to privacy concerns, noting that Meta's servers remain the primary source of latency. The experiment raises questions about whether consumers would be better served by programmable developer kits rather than locked-down commercial hardware like Meta's forthcoming Muse Charm.
takeaways: **Hardware Specifications:** The DIY build used the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C, a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China that lacks cameras and a 5G cellular radio.
**Cost & Setup:** The hardware cost $50 and was paired with Meta's open-source Muse AI cloud using code and tokens from Meta's GitHub, facilitated by Claude Code.
**Audio and Voice Modifications:** Default audio responses were upgraded by plugging in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs' free tier and adding a conversation history swipe feature.

**Custom Software Features:** Claude Code added a Tamagotchi minigame with four levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt, a working three-hand pocket watch face built in 15 minutes, a remote phone camera shutter, and a local video player.
**Security Precautions:** The device was placed on a guest Wi-Fi network immediately following reports that Meta's Muse agent leaked a reviewer's home address.

title: Nvidia weighs playing the cosigner for Nscale’s AI data center in West Virginia
author: Aditya Mehta
contentSnippet:
Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s planned Anthropic data center in West Virginia, The Information reported Thursday . Bloomberg later corroborated the report. Anthropic has signed a $44.6 billion contract for the project’s first building alone, according to Nscale’s IPO filing . In essence, the chipmaker would be co-signing a customer’s loans, a sign of how hard the AI industry is working to keep its buildout plans afloat as investors grow jittery about the amounts of money involved.

The proposed arrangement would help Nscale secure financing for the electricity and construction costs of its West Virginia campus. Under what’s known as a residual value guarantee, Nvidia would step in if Nscale defaulted on construction payments, temporarily take over the facility, and help find a buyer and new tenant, according to The Information .

Nvidia’s earlier support for cloud providers has mostly covered leases and chip purchases, not construction.

The stakes are high for Nscale, which is seeking to go public at a valuation of up to $35 billion despite growing concerns about its ability to deliver on ambitious data center projects.

Anthropic’s contract with Nscale covers the first 460-megawatt building at Nscale’s West Virginia campus, which is expected to use Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips. The companies are also discussing a second deal worth roughly $45 billion for another building.

Nscale has struggled to get its projects off the ground. The company had about 25,000 advanced AI chips running in August , a fraction of the nearly 500,000 it plans to deploy. Its West Virginia campus has run into trouble of its own. Runoff from the construction site has flooded nearby homes more than once . In September, after months of negotiations , the project won state certification.

This month, Microsoft pulled out of a planned Nscale site in England after grid power for it was pushed into the 2030s.

Nvidia has been a major financial backer of the sector, extending roughly $170 billion in investments and credit support to neoclouds and large customers, according to The Information. That includes $1 billion in convertible financing committed to Nscale in September.

Neoclouds, which rent out AI computing power without a cash-rich core business behind them, have come under pressure from investors. Shares of Co

summary.tldr:
Nvidia is currently negotiating a residual value guarantee to back billions in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s data center project in West Virginia. This arrangement would see Nvidia act as a co-signer, assuming control of the facility and finding a new tenant should Nscale default on construction or electricity payments. The project is anchored by a $44.6 billion contract with Anthropic for the first 460-megawatt building, which is slated to utilize Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips. A potential second deal of similar scale is also under discussion.

This move represents a shift in Nvidia’s support strategy, moving beyond standard chip purchase and lease guarantees into direct construction debt backing. The intervention highlights the financial strain on 'neocloud' providers, which lack the cash-rich core businesses of hyperscalers and have seen significant stock declines in October. Nscale, which is targeting an IPO valuation of up to $35 billion, currently operates approximately 25,000 AI chips against a target of 500,000. The West Virginia site has faced operational hurdles, including construction runoff flooding local homes and grid power delays that recently caused Microsoft to abandon a separate Nscale project in England.
takeaways: **Financial Exposure:** Nvidia has extended approximately $170 billion in total investments and credit support to neoclouds and large customers to date.
**Contract Scale:** Anthropic’s initial contract for the first West Virginia building is valued at $44.6 billion, with a potential second building deal valued at roughly $45 billion.
**Hardware Specs:** The West Virginia facility is designed to deploy Nvidia’s upcoming Vera Rubin architecture chips.
**Market Context:** Nscale is seeking an IPO valuation of up to $35 billion, despite having only 25,000 active AI chips as of August against a 500,000-unit deployment goal.

**Credit Risk:** Anthropic faces potential 'junk' credit ratings post-IPO, which may increase its borrowing costs and necessitate reliance on stronger partners like Nvidia to secure infrastructure financing.

title: Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry
author: Tim Fernholz
contentSnippet:
Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.

The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications.

After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus:

Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨

Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite.

A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally.

The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools.

Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation.

If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links.

Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent

summary.tldr:
Google has successfully deployed its 'Suncatcher' prototype satellite, a space-based data center platform launched via a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. The satellite is equipped with four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates 1 kW of electricity. Due to power constraints, the system can operate only one TPU at a time for approximately 20-minute intervals. The project aims to validate the feasibility of performing large-scale AI inference in orbit, with the satellite successfully running Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4 model to generate text and report on orbital conditions.

The primary technical objective of the Suncatcher mission is to evaluate hardware performance under thermal stress and space radiation. Researchers are specifically monitoring for 'bit flips'—radiation-induced memory errors that can corrupt data without triggering standard diagnostic tools. While ground-based simulations suggest radiation impacts are manageable for inference, this mission provides the first real-world data. If successful, Google plans to launch two additional satellites in 2027 featuring enhanced power generation and inter-satellite optical links to support distributed workloads, distinguishing the project from competitors like Starcloud and Cowboy Space, which focus on isolated satellite inference.
takeaways: **Hardware Specs:** The Suncatcher satellite carries four TPUs but is limited to running one at a time due to a 1 kW power generation ceiling.
**Model Deployment:** The satellite successfully executed Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4 model to perform inference tasks, including generating poetry and orbital telemetry reports.
**Radiation Testing:** The mission is actively monitoring for bit flips in memory caused by space radiation, which can corrupt data without triggering traditional monitoring software.
**Future Roadmap:** Google plans a follow-up mission in 2027 involving two satellites equipped with inter-satellite optical links to enable coherent distributed computing.
**Economic Context:** Suncatcher researchers estimate that SpaceX must achieve 1,800 Starship launches to realize the same cost-reduction curves seen with previous launch vehicles.

title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
author: Chris Porter
contentSnippet:
While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens.

Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI.

Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on.

The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies. “As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.”

Terabits a Second, Processed in Flight

Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold.

At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI , a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther , a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS .

Nexus , a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natura

summary.tldr:
Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute have integrated agentic AI into the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California to automate the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. By utilizing NVIDIA’s Holoscan platform, the observatory can now process terabits of sensor data per second in flight, allowing AI agents to steer antennae, calibrate instruments, and perform real-time signal analysis based on natural language prompts. This shift moves the search from manual, storage-heavy workflows to autonomous, compute-intensive pipelines capable of identifying signals in hours rather than weeks or years.

The technical architecture relies on the DAQIRI library to stream data directly into GPU memory, bypassing traditional hard drive storage bottlenecks. The CyberEther framework, built on NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries like cuFFT and cuBLAS, handles signal processing, while the Nexus web-based orchestrator serves as the agent harness. The system currently operates on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, supporting throughput of 2.4 terabits per second. The pipeline has already successfully demonstrated real-time detection of a pulsar in the Crab Nebula, with future plans to deploy open models like NVIDIA Nemotron for offline operations, including potential lunar-based observatories.
takeaways: **System Throughput:** The Allen Telescope Array's new pipeline processes 2.4 terabits per second using NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs.
**Core Software Stack:** The system utilizes the DAQIRI library for data ingestion, CyberEther for signal processing, and Nexus as the natural language-driven agent orchestrator.
**Computational Efficiency:** By processing data in flight via GPU memory, the system replaces weeks or years of manual analysis with hours of autonomous agentic processing.
**Proven Capability:** The pipeline achieved the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar, specifically targeting the Crab Nebula.
**Future Roadmap:** Researchers are evaluating NVIDIA Nemotron for offline deployment scenarios, including potential observatories on the far side of the moon.

title: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity
author: Lucas Ropek
contentSnippet:
French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and governments to download and deploy the system themselves. Nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the model was first introduced earlier this month .

The release comes as competition between open-weight AI developers like Mistral and closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic heats up, with the former arguing that businesses and governments shouldn’t have to rely on outside AI companies for access to advanced capabilities. That argument may hold more weight in cybersecurity, where organizations want more control over their data and systems.

Or, as Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, explained, AI should “be a tool for empowerment, not dominance.” With Chonk, Mistral doubles down on that position, arguing that it’s able to achieve “state-of-the-art performance” at a “fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs.”

The release of the model’s weights — the numerical training that animates the system — ensures that other companies and government agencies will now be able to deploy ML4 for their own purposes.

Mistral says that its model is comparable in terms of performance with a Chinese open-weight competitor, GLM-5.3, which was previously considered one of the best open-weight models in the world — particularly when it comes to cyber work. However, Mistral’s model uses 47 percent fewer tokens per task, making it significantly more economical than GLM-5.3.

The company also claims that the model outranks all other open models when it comes to agentic coding tasks on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, an AI benchmarking site.

French AI developer Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), internally nicknamed “Le Chonk.” The release allows enterprises and government agencies to download and deploy the model on-premise, providing a sovereign alternative to closed-source frontier models from providers like OpenAI and Anthropic. Mistral emphasizes that this open-weight strategy is specifically designed to empower organizations to maintain control over their data and infrastructure, particularly for cybersecurity applications where reliance on third-party API access is considered a security risk.

title: Mistral releases open weights for Mistral Large 4, providing sovereign control for the company’s ‘Le Chonk’ AI model
author: Kyt Dotson
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 11:20 EDT / OCTOBER 29 2026

Mistral releases open weights for Mistral Large 4, providing sovereign control for the company’s ‘Le Chonk’ AI model

Mistral AI SAS today announced the availability of the open weights of its frontier model Mistral Large 4, nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the company’s most capable large language model to date, initially released in preview three weeks ago.

With 1 trillion parameters and 52 billion active parameters, ML4 is natively multimodal and has received three additional weeks of reinforcement training and customer testing. The company says it’s becoming one of the best open agentic coding models in the world, offering leading performance at a small fraction of the token cost with state-of-the-art cyber defense capabilities.

“ML4 OSS showcases our science team’s ability to innovate at speed,” said Vice President of Science Pierre Stock. “Building on the ML4 Preview, the open-weight version continues reinforcement learning training and delivers substantial gains with no signs of saturation.”

The company trained ML4 on 3,800 Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell graphics processing units in its European data centers to achieve high-fidelity performance for tool use and coding, driven by end-to-end control of its infrastructure and the ability to optimize for hardware during model development.

Open weights mean companies can take the model and deploy it on their own hardware, within their own firewalls, and run sensitive data without exposing it to the cloud or outside parties. With Mistral’s model, companies will have a Western-developed model to compete with the multitude of ultra-large Chinese coding models on the market, such as the GLM family from Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co. Ltd. and the Kimi family from Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co. Ltd.

“Open source is essential to ensure state-of-the-art AI does not end up concentrated in the hands of a few actors,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Arthur Mensch. “Other labs have raised hundreds of billions to develop equivalent capabilities; in three years, Mistral raised roughly $6 billion.”

Because of its training regimen, ML4 stands out among many other frontier models, rivaling even top models such as Chinese-built GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average.

On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which tests agentic coding

summary.tldr:
Mistral AI has released the open weights for its frontier model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), internally nicknamed "Le Chonk." The model features 1 trillion total parameters with 52 billion active parameters and is natively multimodal. Following a three-week preview period, the open-weight version incorporates additional reinforcement learning and customer testing, positioning it as a high-performance agentic coding model designed for sovereign deployment within private enterprise firewalls.

Technically, ML4 was trained on 3,800 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs in European data centers, allowing for hardware-level optimization. The model introduces three distinct reasoning modes—low, medium, and high—enabling users to adjust reasoning depth per task without prompt engineering. On the Terminal-Bench 4.0 benchmark, ML4 achieved a 41% score, tying with the Chinese-built GLM-5.3 for top performance in agentic coding while reportedly consuming 47% fewer tokens per task on average.

**Reasoning Control:** The model includes three selectable reasoning modes (low, medium, high) to manage token consumption and depth for specific enterprise workloads.
**Strategic Positioning:** The release is intended to provide a Western-developed alternative to Chinese coding models like Zhipu AI's GLM and Moonshot AI's Kimi.

title: Trump DOE loans $5B to nuclear plants that will power data centers
author: Tim De Chant
contentSnippet:
The Trump administration is giving Constellation Energy $5 billion in loans to expand nuclear generating capacity at eight power plants by 1.1 gigawatts.

Most or all of the additional power from seven of those facilities has already been bought by Google, Meta, or Amazon.

Constellation said it plans to use the financing to “uprate” 11 existing reactors, an industry term for expanding capacity at a reactor, often by using more highly enriched uranium and by upgrading equipment to handle the increased power levels.

The energy company said it had already committed to spending more than $7 billion to add 1,080 megawatts of nuclear capacity to deliver power to Google, Amazon, and Meta. The loan commitment, which has yet to be finalized, “could lower financing costs” for the projects, Constellation said in a press release .

The eight power plants include six in Illinois (Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, La Salle, and Quad Cities), one in Maryland (Calvert Cliffs), and one in Pennsylvania (Limerick).

Google is already the confirmed buyer of additional power from the Pennsylvania plant and four Illinois power plants, while Amazon is buying electricity from the Maryland plant and Meta is effectively buying the entire Clinton power plant in Illinois.

On Tuesday, the Department of Energy touted the loan as supporting “affordable, reliable power to American homes and businesses,” though there is no evidence that the new nuclear capacity will lower prices for residential ratepayers. Constellation’s announcement does not say whether the projects will maintain or lower electricity rates, and the company would not confirm the government’s claim to TechCrunch.

Hyperscalers, including Google, Amazon, and Meta, have been scouring the grid for additional capacity to support their AI data centers. Tech companies are paying handsomely for energy, committing tens of billions of dollars over the coming years. Given that power has become a competitive advantage, that estimate is probably on the low end.

By lowering the cost of capital for the upgrades, the Department of Energy’s loans could boost Constellation’s bottom line, that of the hyperscalers — or both.

title: Dual DeltaNet: Value-Side Memory Reorganization for Linear Attention
author: Yixiao Qian
contentSnippet:
Authors: Yixiao Qian , Yaxin Zhang , Song Chen , Jiaxu Liu , Shengze Cai , Chao Xu

Abstract: Linear attention and state space models (SSMs) offer efficient alternatives to softmax attention by maintaining a fixed-size recurrent state, but this design requires careful management to preserve useful historical associations and limit interference. The delta rule helps reduce interference through correction of the value associated with each key, but it does not explicitly account for how related value features are distributed across the state. We observe that a state $\boldsymbol{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k\times d_v}$ can be viewed as a bank of $d_k$ addresses storing $d_v$-dimensional values. While a key-side read $\boldsymbol{S}^\top\boldsymbol{k}$ retrieves the value associated with $\boldsymbol{k}$, a value-side read $\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{e}$ aggregates addresses whose stored value features match the selector $\boldsymbol{e}$. Based on this observation, we propose Dual DeltaNet (DDN), which extends Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) with a two-sided delta rule. The key-side delta rule reads with the current key to correct its associated value, while the complementary value-side delta rule reads with selected features of the current value to reorganize the addresses it occupies. We derive a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence that increases arithmetic intensity during inference. Compared with KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3, DDN achieves the strongest overall performance across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks, and retrieval, while incurring modest training and inference overhead relative to KDA. Code: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers Yixiao Qian, Yaxin Zhang, Song Chen, Jiaxu Liu, Shengze Cai, and Chao Xu have introduced Dual DeltaNet (DDN), a novel architecture designed to improve linear attention mechanisms by addressing the limitations of standard state-space models (SSMs) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). The model conceptualizes the internal state as a bank of $d_k$ addresses storing $d_v$-dimensional values, allowing for both key-side reads (retrieving values via keys) and value-side reads (aggregating addresses via feature selectors). By implementing a two-sided delta rule, DDN corrects values based on keys while simultaneously reorganizing the addresses occupied by value features, effectively reducing historical interference.

Technically, DDN extends the KDA framework by incorporating a complementary value-side delta rule that operates alongside the traditional key-side correction. The authors derived a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence mechanism, which enhances arithmetic intensity during inference compared to existing linear attention models. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that DDN outperforms KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3 across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks, and retrieval benchmarks. While the model introduces additional complexity, the authors report that the performance gains are achieved with only modest increases in training and inference overhead.
takeaways: **Core Innovation:** Dual DeltaNet (DDN) introduces a two-sided delta rule that performs both key-side value correction and value-side address reorganization.
**State Representation:** The model treats the state matrix $\boldsymbol{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k \times d_v}$ as a memory bank where $d_k$ addresses store $d_v$-dimensional values.
**Inference Optimization:** The architecture utilizes a rank-2 recurrence to increase arithmetic intensity during inference, improving efficiency over standard linear attention.
**Performance Benchmarks:** DDN demonstrates superior performance compared to KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3 in language modeling, zero-shot tasks, and retrieval.
**Implementation:** The authors have provided a chunkwise parallel training algorithm to facilitate efficient model scaling.

title: Learning to Code the World: Harness Evolution for Compositional 3D Reconstruction
author: Haoyu Yao
contentSnippet:
Authors: Haoyu Yao , Chenguo Lin , Ruize Du , Yadong Mu

Abstract: Reconstructing editable and compositional 3D scenes from a real image requires jointly reasoning about geometry, object structure, and spatial relationships. We introduce SceneEvolve, a framework that represents 3D scenes as executable code and improves reconstruction by evolving the harness around a small open-source agent. SceneEvolve combines SceneAct, a compositional semantic action interface built on parameterized primitives, hierarchical composition, and semantic spatial relations, with SceneHarness-RSI, which leverages a stronger teacher agent to iteratively evolve the harness using feedback from development-set reconstructions. Throughout harness evolution, the model parameters, action semantics, and execution backend remain fixed. The resulting harness provides a reusable reconstruction procedure that enables the small open-source model to reconstruct unseen scenes without parameter updates or teacher assistance. Across two in-domain datasets and one out-of-domain dataset, SceneEvolve with the comparatively compact Qwen3.8-27B model improves all four evaluated reconstruction metrics while reducing mean inference time by 47.0% relative to the base model. More notably, despite relying on a substantially smaller model, SceneEvolve achieves 32.3% higher reconstruction quality than the large proprietary GPT-5.6-Sol model, while reducing mean equivalent deployment cost by 59.8%. Furthermore, the harness evolved using Qwen3.8-27B also generalizes to Kimi-K3, achieving comparable reconstruction performance to GPT-6-Astra. The project page is this https URL .

summary.tldr:
Researchers Haoyu Yao, Chenguo Lin, Ruize Du, and Yadong Mu have introduced SceneEvolve, a framework for compositional 3D scene reconstruction that represents scenes as executable code. The system utilizes SceneAct, a semantic action interface based on parameterized primitives and hierarchical composition, alongside SceneHarness-RSI, which employs a teacher agent to iteratively refine the reconstruction harness. By keeping model parameters, action semantics, and the execution backend fixed, the framework enables a small open-source agent to perform complex 3D reconstructions without requiring further parameter updates or ongoing teacher assistance.

In performance evaluations, the SceneEvolve framework paired with the Qwen3.8-27B model outperformed the large proprietary GPT-5.6-Sol model, achieving 32.3% higher reconstruction quality while simultaneously reducing mean deployment costs by 59.8%. The system also demonstrated significant efficiency gains, cutting mean inference time by 47.0% compared to the base model. Furthermore, the harness evolved via Qwen3.8-27B showed cross-model generalization, allowing the Kimi-K3 model to reach reconstruction performance levels comparable to GPT-6-Astra.

**Comparative Performance:** SceneEvolve with Qwen3.8-27B achieves 32.3% higher reconstruction quality than the proprietary GPT-5.6-Sol model.
